clue.text: Jack says it's bad for us to complain slangily by 'phone, having lost Rover as well

definitions.text: Jack says it's bad for us

parts.note: to beef is slang for to grumble or complain

indicators.note: having lost tells us some words drop out of the phrase

parts.note: dog and bone is rhyming slang for phone, so 'by phone' is 'on the dog and bone'
Rover is a typical dog's name, and 'as well' gives AND, so together the words 'dog and' are removed

explanation.surface: A minister named Jack complains about something harmful, phoning it in while missing his dog or his car.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cunningham, the UK agriculture minister, banned the sale of beef on the bone in 1997 over BSE fears. 'By phone' is ON THE DOG AND BONE in rhyming slang; 'having lost' Rover (DOG) and 'as well' (AND) leaves ONTHEBONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1997 ban rested on the government's claim that such meat was a health risk to consumers.

clue.text: Puerile? Oh, could be Edward Heath for one

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might form something else when rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking if childish behaviour fits the former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' tells you PUERILE plus OH can be rearranged. Edward Heath, Conservative PM 1970-74, took Britain into the European Community.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath was the most committed pro-European of British prime ministers, an example of an enthusiast for Europe.

clue.text: Really great getting one over an old-style socialist!

parts.note: fab is slang, short for fabulous
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Delight at gaining the upper hand over a traditional left-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society, founded 1884, championed gradual socialism; it predates New Labour by a century.
explanation.definitionFit: A Fabian is a member of the Fabian Society, a long-established British gradualist socialist group.

clue.text: Stupid arse in collar, your next of kin?

definitions.note: as a noun phrase, 'your nearest' means your closest relatives, as in 'nearest and dearest'

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the word for collar

parts.note: to collar a criminal is to net or catch them

indicators.note: stupid means muddled, so the letters of arse are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether the idiot in the dog collar is a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: Your nearest are your closest family, the relatives who count as next of kin.

clue.text: Use Thatcher-type negotiating tactics, giving worker the sack!

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
a bag is a sack

explanation.surface: Bargaining like Margaret Thatcher by firing an employee.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher's handbag became a symbol of her bossy style, and 'to handbag' entered British English as a verb for browbeating.
explanation.definitionFit: To handbag someone is to bully or berate them, the hectoring style Thatcher used in negotiations.

clue.text: Church gives Nadir interest in cab renovation

indicators.note: in places the tycoon's first name and the abbreviation inside the rebuilt letters
renovation means doing up, so the letters of cab are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Asil Nadir, the Polly Peck tycoon who fled to Cyprus in 1993
I is the abbreviation for interest in finance

explanation.surface: A disgraced tycoon's money pays for doing up a taxi, while a church benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nadir' looks like the lowest point; it is Asil Nadir, the Polly Peck tycoon who fled Britain in 1993. 'Renovation' rebuilds the cab's letters to BCA, and his first name plus I goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A basilica is a large oblong church, often one granted special status by the Pope.

clue.text: See 8
Massive erection, an unnecessary diversion for the Tyneside motorist?

definitions.text: Massive erection, an unnecessary diversion for the Tyneside motorist?

parts.words: Massive erection, an unnecessary diversion for the Tyneside motorist?
parts.note: the giant steel sculpture by the A1 at Gateshead, a distraction for drivers; erection means a built structure, with a smutty double meaning

explanation.walkthrough: Antony Gormley's 20-metre steel sculpture was put up in 1998 beside the A1 near Gateshead. 'Diversion' means a distraction for drivers, not a road detour, and 'unnecessary' is the Eye's sneer at the cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The sculpture is a huge winged figure erected on a hill overlooking the main road into Tyneside.

clue.text: Messenger possibly having got things off chest in tabloid paper

definitions.text: Messenger possibly having got things off chest in tabloid paper

parts.words: Messenger possibly having got things off chest in tabloid paper
parts.note: a page can be a messenger boy, and the topless model of the Sun's third page has literally taken things off her chest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Got things off chest' sounds like confessing; it means removing clothing. The Sun printed a topless model on its third page from 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: A page three girl was a topless glamour model pictured in a British tabloid newspaper.

clue.text: Hear Brian's dithering half-wit

indicators.note: dithering means wavering and shaky, so the letters are unsettled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the name Brian, the 's linking it to what follows

explanation.surface: Listen to a man called Brian hesitating like a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A harebrain is a scatterbrained, foolish person, a synonym for a half-wit.

clue.text: Tony finally appears in broadcasts backing the country

indicators.note: appears in tells us the letter sits inside the reversed word
backing means going backwards, so the word for broadcasts is read in reverse

parts.note: airs means broadcasts, as a programme is aired

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the name Tony

parts.note: the last letter of Tony

explanation.surface: Tony Blair turns up at last in news broadcasts supporting a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a Middle Eastern nation, a straightforward example of a country.

clue.text: On taking a piss, we hear, in section of church, do a Chamberlain impersonation

indicators.note: taking means the church section takes the sound-alike word into itself

parts.note: the apse is the rounded end section of a church

indicators.note: we hear signals a word spelt differently but said the same, pee sounding like the vegetable pea

parts.note: a pee, a piss

explanation.surface: Someone relieves themselves in a church, then imitates a former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' gives PEA, the vegetable that sounds like a pee, and the church section is 'taking' it. Neville Chamberlain is remembered for appeasing Hitler at Munich in 1938.
explanation.definitionFit: Chamberlain's Munich policy is the textbook case of conciliating an aggressor by concession.

clue.text: Bloody-minded sort creating personal stink — left the girl holding one

parts.note: BO is body odour, a personal smell

indicators.note: holding means the word for the girl has the numeral inside it

parts.note: she refers to a girl
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An obstinate person kicks up a stink, then walks out on his girlfriend while she clutches something.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl 'holding' one makes SHIE. Bolshie is British slang, shortened from Bolshevik, for stroppy or uncooperative.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolshie describes an awkward, contrary attitude, and it is used as a noun for such a person.

clue.text: Smooth-talking, grand old politician

parts.note: G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand pounds
Lib is short for Liberal, the old party merged into the Liberal Democrats in 1988

explanation.surface: A distinguished elderly politician with a silver tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Glib describes fluent but shallow speech, the manner of someone persuasive and insincere.

clue.text: Ford's classic cowboy transport outfit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: John Ford's classic 1939 Western film
second meaning: ..., the British bus and rail company, jibed at as a cowboy (dodgy) firm, with a pun on the Wild West vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: Ford is the film director, not the car maker. 'Cowboy' in British usage means a shoddy or unscrupulous operator, which the Eye applied to the bus company Stagecoach.
explanation.definitionFit: The film title and the company name are the same, and both evoke the horse-drawn coach of Western movies.

clue.text: A not quite fatuously senile appliance?

indicators.note: not quite tells us the word is a letter short

parts.note: gaga means foolishly senile

explanation.surface: Asking whether an elderly person going a bit soft in the head is a gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: GAGA is 'not quite' complete: drop its first G. The opening 'A' is just part of the surface. An Aga is a heavy British cast-iron range cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aga is a brand of cooking stove, a large kitchen appliance.

clue.text: The bloke's in the room at the top, denying the man upstairs

indicators.note: in places the contraction inside the room at the top

parts.note: the attic is the room at the top of a house
the bloke's expands to 'he is', the bloke being he

explanation.surface: A man is in the loft denying there is anyone upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bloke's' gives HE IS, which goes 'in' ATTIC after its first two letters. 'The man upstairs' is a folksy name for God, which ties neatly to the attic in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheistic outlook rejects the existence of God, colloquially 'the man upstairs'.

clue.text: Bury: clear favourite with surfers!

parts.note: to inter is to bury
net means clear, as in net profit after deductions

explanation.surface: Bury, the Lancashire town, is described as a clear favourite with surfers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' with a capital looks like the Lancashire town; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Surfing the web is browsing online, so web surfers favour the global computer network.

clue.text: Be like a national leader unalive to public scrutiny

definitions.text: Be like a national leader unalive to public scrutiny

parts.words: Be like a national leader unalive to public scrutiny
parts.note: a dead head of state is displayed so the public can file past the coffin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unalive' is the joke: the leader is dead, and the coffin is laid out for public view rather than the leader being subjected to scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A deceased dignitary's body is placed on public display before the funeral, a ceremonial honour.

clue.text: Lech indiscriminately, knock around and you might get this

indicators.note: around places the light knock on either side of the scrambled letters

parts.note: a tap is a light knock

indicators.note: indiscriminately means without order, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sleep around with no care and you could catch a disease.
explanation.walkthrough: Lech mixed 'indiscriminately' gives HECL, with the knock 'around' it. The clue doubles as the story: indiscriminate lechery is exactly how this infection is caught.
explanation.definitionFit: The clap is slang for gonorrhoea, a sexually transmitted infection caught from promiscuity.

clue.text: Taken by those choosing to avoid the issue of sex

definitions.text: Taken by those choosing to avoid the issue of sex

parts.words: Taken by those choosing to avoid the issue of sex
parts.note: the oral contraceptive is taken by women who want to avoid having children; issue means offspring

explanation.walkthrough: 'Avoid the issue' sounds like dodging a topic; issue means children, the result of sex.
explanation.definitionFit: The contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy, so it is taken to avoid conceiving.

clue.text: A broad brogue, perhaps? "Bugger off!", you say

indicators.note: you say signals a word with the same sound but different spelling

parts.note: shoo is what you say to drive someone away

explanation.surface: A thick Irish accent tells someone rudely to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You say' means SHOO said aloud. 'Brogue' looks like an accent, given 'broad'; it is the sturdy leather footwear, and a broad one is wide-fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A brogue is a type of leather lace-up, so it is an example of footwear, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Put money on Bill getting stress

indicators.note: on means the money word is put after the word for bill, following it in the answer

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill
a cent is a coin, a small sum of money

explanation.surface: Betting on someone called Bill causes anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' looks like worry; it is emphasis in speech. 'On' puts the money after the bill, and 'Put' only joins the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is the emphasis placed on a syllable when speaking.

clue.text: A camera lens angle linked to an organ

parts.note: to angle is to fish with rod and line
the eye is an organ of the body

explanation.surface: A photography lens set at an angle joined to part of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angle' looks like a camera term; it is the verb for fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisheye is an ultra-wide photographic lens giving a strongly curved image.

clue.text: US ambassador embraces Latin American piece

indicators.note: embraces means the phrase holds the word within it

parts.note: the letters run across both words

explanation.surface: An American envoy hugs a piece of South American music.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a Brazilian dance, and a piece of its music is a samba.

clue.text: Throwing up — not right impression

indicators.note: not tells us a letter is left out of the word

parts.note: retching is heaving as if to vomit

explanation.surface: Someone being sick gives the wrong idea.
explanation.walkthrough: RETCHING with 'not' R. 'Impression' sounds like an opinion, but it is a print taken from an etched plate.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a print made from an acid-bitten metal plate, so it is an impression in the printmaker's sense.

clue.text: Virgin's fragile barrier means Carol possibly has to go round tail of airplane

indicators.note: has to go round means the hymn surrounds the letter that follows

parts.note: a carol is one example of a hymn, hence 'possibly'

indicators.note: tail of means the last letter of the word airplane

parts.note: the last letter of airplane

explanation.surface: A girl named Carol must circle an aircraft's tail, the clue suggests, to keep her virginity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has to go round' puts HYMN, the carol, around E, the 'tail of' airplane.
explanation.definitionFit: The hymen is the membrane traditionally associated with virginity.

clue.text: The old queen's favourite jockey familiarly imbibing the hard stuff

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the jockey takes the frozen water inside

parts.note: Lester Piggott, the great jockey, known simply by his first name
ice is water in its hard state; 'the hard stuff' usually means spirits

explanation.surface: An elderly monarch's favourite rider has been drinking spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: LESTER 'imbibing' ICE. 'The hard stuff' suggests whisky; it is ice. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was Elizabeth I's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of Leicester was Queen Elizabeth I's closest courtier and rumoured suitor.

clue.text: Do affairs represent the self-serving activities of Labour, Tory, etc, groups?

definitions.text: the self-serving activities of Labour, Tory, etc, groups

parts.note: a do is a party, a social gathering
politics means the affairs of government

explanation.surface: Asking whether scandalous liaisons sum up the conduct of Britain's political parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affairs' suggests sexual scandal; here it means public affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Party politics is manoeuvring for the advantage of one's own faction rather than the public good.
